strengths: The paper addresses a practical failure mode in parallax stitching. Repairing misaligned regions near an existing seam, while preserving its boundary labels, is an intuitive and potentially useful extension to existing seam-cutting pipelines.

The controlled evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets and four seam-cutting methods. Table I reports consistent improvements across all four metrics; for example, Perception’s SSIM on SEAGULL increases from 0.613 to 0.682. The visual examples also demonstrate useful local repairs.
The pipeline is illustrated clearly, established components and datasets are cited, and a code/data link is provided. The implementation information and explicit failure examples are helpful.
weaknesses: The originality is insufficiently established relative to the cited seam-quality evaluation method [19], seam-guided local alignment [25], and dense-matching-based seam estimation [21]. Section II.B’s characterization of previous approaches as operating on settled alignments is overly broad, including relative to its own descriptions of those methods. The distinctive contribution of the proposed local repair strategy needs sharper justification.

The experiments establish improvements over seam cutting on REW-aligned images, but provide limited evidence against closely related alignment-and-seam approaches. Parallax and SEAGULL receive only a single qualitative comparison in Fig. 6, and [21] is not evaluated. Beyond the single illustrative flow-modification example in Fig. 3, there are no dataset-level ablations establishing the contributions of patch selection, flow modification, and constrained seam merging.

The evaluation primarily measures agreement between image patches along the selected seam. These metrics are relevant but do not adequately establish final mosaic quality or preservation of scene geometry. Per-image outcomes, artifact assessments, or perceptual evaluation would help determine whether average improvements conceal damaging local distortions.

The detector can classify uniformly poor seams as plausible because it tests max(Q) against 1.5 times mean(Q). Figure 7 also documents difficulties merging small patches smoothly. These acknowledged limitations affect the module’s central detection-and-repair function, but their frequency and sensitivity to thresholds and patch size are not quantified. Section III.B’s assertion that false positives cannot worsen results is consequently unsupported.

The central warp is ambiguously specified: Eq. (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Eq. (5) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized spatial position. The actual displacement-weighting operation and boundary treatment need clarification, alongside patch-padding and SIFT-flow settings. This may be repairable notation and implementation detail, but currently limits reproducibility.

The efficiency claim lacks a convincing comparative basis. Table III reports roughly 7–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, often exceeding the original non-iterative seam-cutting cost. Alignment time is excluded, and no end-to-end timing against the seam-guided alternatives establishes the proposed approach’s computational advantage.
